 The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping
 4 out of 5 stars A new hero arises in this exciting and stacked Hunger Games prequel Film 
 Recommended 
 Tuesday 17 November 2026 Share Copy Link Facebook Twitter Pinterest Email WhatsApp Written by Phil de Semlyen Global film editor Advertising Time Out says
 The Hunger Games movies long outlasted their dystopian rivals ( Divergent , anyone?) on the back of their Oscars-minted casts and a steadfast unwillingness to let audiences off the hook. Suzanne Collins’ stories are as dark as young adult sci-fi comes, topical interrogations of tyrannical societies and guilty-pleasure reflections of our need for entertainment, no matter how bleak. This one arrives a matter of weeks after the US government floated the idea of broadcasting a live execution on TV. Sci-fi? Hardly. 
 The latest – directed by Hunger Games veteran Francis Lawrence, based on Collins’ 2025 novel and set 24 years before Jennifer Lawrence’s Katniss first entered the arena – is as strong as any of the five movies before it, an origin story that deepens the stories’ lore and doubles down on those original principles.   
 It’s certainly a major step up from 2023’s drab prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes – and the absence of Lawrence isn’t felt as keenly for the focus on Aussie actor Joseph Zada as Haymitch Abernathy, the Woody Harrelson character of the original trilogy and, on this evidence, Panem’s answer to Elvis.  
 A tousled dreamboat with a kind soul and caring nature, he’s ripped from his family and girlfriend (Whitney Peak) and sent to represent the Rust Belt-ish District 12 in the beefed-up Quarter Quell. Joining him are boyhood friend Louella McCoy (Molly McCann) and bookie’s son Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), who freaks out the other tributes by giving running odds on their survival chances. Mckenna Grace’s furnace-tempered, sarcastic twin Maysilee Donner channels the spirit of Katniss as the fourth representative of their downtrodden district. Her run-in with Glenn Close’s gloriously grotesque Capitol escort Drusilla Sickle is a vicious early highlight. 
 Kieran Culkin was born to play someone called Caesar Flickerman
 Frankly, you’d watch this film just for the cast. Replacing Donald Sutherland as Snow, Philip Seymour Hoffman’s scheming spin doctor Plutarch Heavensbee and Stanley Tucci’s TV compère, Francis Lawrence can call on Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons and Kieran Culkin. Fiennes brings considered menace, Plemons a shifty brand of media savvy and Culkin was born to play someone called Caesar Flickerman. Elle Fanning is flamboyant as emerging couture queen Effie Trinket, though Billy Ray and Michael Lesslie’s script doesn’t find much time for Maya Hawke, Kelvin Harrison Jr and Lili Taylor as previous winners-turned-mentors with very little mentoring to do. 
 In the wake of the Wicked movies, the franchise feels even more like a twisted, blood-lusting take on The Wizard of Oz. Here, the Emerald City is a viper’s nest presided over by a younger but no less venomous President Snow. The seeds are cleverly planted for the rebellion to come in later stories, weaknesses in Panem’s power structures laid bare even as Haymitch finds that being the present at the birth of a rebellion is a death sentence.  
 At two-and-a-half hours, Sunrise on the Reaping ’s runtime could have used some reaping of its own. The leggier second half, in which Haymitch and Maysilee team up to survive an arena in which even the bunnies are lethal, isn’t as interesting as the Capitol’s blur of late-Rome decadence, bustling energy and political chicanery. 
 But Sunrise on the Reaping is far stronger than so many fished-from-the-bin franchise revivals. The filmmaker has three other Hunger Games films on his CV, but none with this level of visual assurance (except for some dodgy CGI in the arena). And it’s more than just a join-the-dots origin tale for Harrelson’s boozily disillusioned but essentially noble Haymitch of the stories to come. The odds continue to be in this enduring franchise’s favour.   
 In cinemas worldwide Fri November 20 .
